en: The Sūtra on the Origin Story of the Great Firm Brahmin Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta, Dharma Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Imperially Conferred the Rank of Chao Feng Da Fu and Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and others, by Imperial Decree. Translated in the Western Heaven (India).
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha together with a great assembly.
At that time, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, having passed the night, arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling at the break of dawn.
His body was radiant with a vast and brilliant light, such that the entire Vulture Peak Mountain became a single mass of radiance.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At one time, while I was in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, I saw Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with Mahābrahmā and the assembly of the gods of the Sudharmā Hall, gathered and engaged in discourse:
"This I have personally heard; this I have personally received."
"What is the meaning of this?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me, so that I may understand it.
The Buddha addressed the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, saying:

"Whatever you have heard and received at the assembly where Śakra, Lord of the Devas of the Thirty-three, Mahābrahmā, and the host of the Heaven of Good Dharma gather, I shall now tell it to you as appropriate, so that you may understand it."
At that time, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
On one occasion, I was at the assembly hall where Śakra, Lord of the Devas of the Thirty-three Heavens, Mahābrahmā, and the host of the Sudharmā devas were gathered together.”
At that time, there may be a son of heaven who, due to certain causes and conditions, is born for the first time in that celestial realm.

Simultaneously, another son of heaven who was born earlier sees this newcomer and gives rise to five kinds of supreme objects of affection and delight: namely, longevity, physical appearance, renown, auspiciousness, and retinue.
“World-Honored One!
Among them, there is a class of devaputras who speak thus: ‘O devaputras!’”

"You all should observe this newly born deva-son; there are other previously born deva-sons who have given rise to five kinds of supreme objects of affection, namely: lifespan, physical form, reputation, auspiciousness, and retinue."
At that time, there was another class of devaputras who spoke as follows: "O devaputras!

This newly born one is one who, within the Dharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) and, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of his life, experienced the retribution of a favorable rebirth and came to be born here in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
At that same time, there were certain sons of gods who gave rise to five kinds of supreme delight.
Then, another class of sons of gods spoke these words:
"How wonderful, O sons of gods!"

There are four Buddha Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who have appeared in the world, proclaiming all dharmas for the benefit of devas and humans, diminishing the hosts of asuras, and increasing the hosts of devas.
At that time, there was another class of devaputras who spoke thus: "Stop! O devaputras!"
It is not that the four Buddha Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have appeared in the world.
How wonderful!
O sons of the gods!

There are three Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who have appeared in the world, proclaiming all dharmas to benefit devas and humans, diminishing the host of asuras, and increasing the host of devas.
At that time, there was another class of devaputras who spoke thus: "Stop! O devaputras!"
It is not that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the three [times] appear in the world.
How wonderful!
O sons of the gods!

There are two Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who have appeared in the world, proclaiming all dharmas to benefit devas and humans, diminishing the hosts of asuras, and increasing the hosts of devas.
“May the Buddha please explain such matters as these.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and Mahābrahmā were present in the assembly. The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra and the host of devas regarding this matter, saying:
“You should know that at one and the same time, there is no place where two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas can appear in the world to proclaim the various dharmas.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the assembly of devas, having heard the Buddha’s words, all gave rise to joy, their hearts and minds feeling great satisfaction.
Then, the World-Honored One, knowing that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the assembly of devas had all become joyful, addressed the multitude, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, appearing in the world, is endowed with eight kinds of rare and marvelous qualities.”
"If you wish to hear it, you should generate a mind of superior joy and give rise to a sense of delight.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!
"Now, for the sake of this assembly of devas, speak as you see fit regarding the eight marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, proclaimed the eight marvelous qualities of the World-Honored One:
"O sons of the gods!..."

Whenever a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, it is certain that the host of asuras will diminish and the host of devas will increase, thereby bringing benefit, welfare, and happiness to many people.
Such benefit and happiness are truly rare.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

As for the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world, I see no difference between the past and the present; therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world to proclaim the teachings of the Dharma, benefiting devas and humans."

These are: the dharma that shatters all views; the dharma that abandons defilement; the dharma that accords with contemplation; the dharma that is pure and white; the dharma that brings full knowledge of all feelings; the dharma that eliminates arrogance; the dharma that subdues the flood of craving; the dharma that destroys ignorance; the dharma that severs dependence; the dharma that leaves behind greedy attachment; the dharma of tranquility; and the dharma of nirvana.
To proclaim all phenomena in this way is truly marvelous.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

Since the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world, I have seen no difference between the past and the present; therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having appeared in the world, teaches the trainings to his śrāvakas—namely, the various dharmas of non-anger that ought to be cultivated.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has repeatedly instructed:

"O practitioners, you should cultivate the practice of non-contention (*araṇā*) in wilderness retreats, quiet places, and the like; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, remain far removed from bustle and free from clamor. Relying upon yourselves, according to your own physical appearance, according to your own inclinations, and according to what you yourself love, do not mingle with others, but act in accordance with your own proper conduct."
To provide such instruction is truly marvelous.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

Since the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world, I have seen no difference between the past and the present; therefore, although the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world and partakes of various foods in accordance with worldly custom, he always obtains the supreme flavor within food, the correct flavor, the foremost flavor, and the flavor that is never dispersed.

Furthermore, the food and drink received by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha are free from pride, without dwelling or attachment; they are always devoid of faults, give rise to right wisdom, and are ever intent on renunciation.
Furthermore, to teach and demonstrate this Dharma to all beings is truly rare.
Moreover, O sons of the gods!

Since the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world, I have seen no difference between the past and the present; therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having appeared in the world and being fully endowed with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), teaches the Dharma of supernormal powers to his śrāvakas, instructing, guiding, and leading them so that they may practice it.
To provide such instruction is truly marvelous.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

Since the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world, I have seen no difference between the past and the present; therefore, the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the world is free from all doubt and free from speculative theories, attaining fearlessness regarding wholesome dharmas. That he is thus free from doubt is itself marvelous.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

I see no difference whatsoever between the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world in the past and his appearance in the present. Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having appeared in the world, is able to practice exactly as he teaches among all dharmas, and is able to teach exactly as he practices; furthermore, by means of these dharmas, he instructs, guides, and leads others so that they may practice them."
Such instruction is truly marvelous.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

Since the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, in the world, I have seen no difference between the past and the present; therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world to teach nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, increasing and fulfilling them without end.

Just as the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers flow into the great ocean and increase there without end, so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: he teaches nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, skillfully expounding all dharmas conducive to nirvāṇa and establishing them well, causing their practice to increase without end.
To provide such instruction is truly rare.
"O sons of the gods!
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has appeared in the world, fully endowed with these eight kinds of rare qualities; therefore, I see no difference between him and those of the past or the present."

At that time, having heard these words, the assembly of devas was even more exalted than before; they all gave rise to joy, their hearts were refreshed, and together they addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, saying:
"Lord of Devas!..."
“We pray that you will once again proclaim for us those eight marvelous qualities of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, proclaimed the eight marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata for that assembly of devas for a second time:
“Furthermore, O sons of the gods!...”

Whenever a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, he invariably causes the host of asuras to diminish and the host of devas to increase; he is able to bring benefit and happiness to many people. Such benefit and happiness are truly rare.
"O sons of the gods!

For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, has appeared in the world; I see no difference between him in the past and in the present. As was explained at length previously, even so, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has appeared in the world to teach nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, increasing and fulfilling it without end."

Just as the waters of the Gaṅgā River and the Yamunā River flow into the great ocean and increase there without end, so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: he teaches nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, skillfully expounds all dharmas pertaining to nirvāṇa, and establishes them well, causing their practice to increase without end.
Such instruction is truly rare.
O sons of the gods!
When the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, appears in the world, he is endowed with these eight rare and marvelous qualities.
"Therefore, I perceive no difference between the past and the present.
Having spoken thus, that assembly of devaputras became even more exalted than before; they all gave rise to joy, their minds feeling refreshed and contented.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the assembly of devaputras had become even more exalted than before and had given rise to joy, again addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!
"Now, once again, proclaim the eight marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, for the third time spoke of the eight marvelous qualities:
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!"

Whenever a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, he invariably causes the host of asuras to diminish and the host of devas to increase, and is able to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to many people.
Such benefit and happiness are truly rare.
O sons of the gods!

Therefore, when the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, appears in the world, I see no difference between him and those of the past or the present. As has been explained at length previously, even unto this: the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world to teach nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, increasing and fulfilling it without end.

Just as the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers flow into the great ocean and increase there without end, so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: he teaches nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, skillfully expounding all dharmas of nirvāṇa and establishing them well, causing their practice to increase without end.
Such an instruction is truly rare.
O sons of the gods!
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, appearing in the world, is fully endowed with these eight rare qualities; therefore, I see no difference between him and those of the past or the present.
When he had spoken thus, the Great Brahmā King,
knowing that the assembly of devas was even more exalted than before and that they all felt joy and their minds were refreshed, spoke these verses:
“The Lord Śakra and the host of devas All give rise to such a heart of joy.”
I take refuge in and praise the Buddha, the Tathāgata, who has excellently expounded the rare Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Having seen in the past one newly born among the gods, endowed with perfect physical marks and majestic radiance,
I know that by having long cultivated the holy life, they have attained birth in that celestial realm possessed of supreme power.
At that time, having heard these verses, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods became even more exalted than before; they all gave rise to joy, and their minds were filled with delight.
Then, the Great Brahmā King, knowing that the celestial assembly had become even more exalted than before and had given rise to joy, addressed the assembly, saying:

"If you wish to hear with delight concerning the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—who possesses great wisdom and has brought much benefit and happiness throughout the long night—then you should give rise to a joyous mind even more exalted than before, and arouse a heart of gladness."
At that time, those hosts of devas addressed the Great Brahmā King, saying:
“Excellent, Great Brahmā King!
We pray only that you will explain at length how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with great wisdom, has brought about benefits and happiness for all throughout the long night.”
At that time, the Great Brahmā King immediately expounded at length for him the causes and conditions of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom from his past lives.
Then, the Brahmā King said:
“World-Honored One!
In a past age long gone by, there was a king named Viṣṇu.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Dṛḍha who served as the minister of state and was the king’s preceptor; he was intelligent and possessed great wisdom, endowed with vast talent and strategy, and was skilled in governing the affairs of the kingdom.
The king had a crown prince named Reṇu, whom the king cherished and held dear; he was intelligent and possessed great wisdom, as well as great talent, and was skilled in managing all affairs.
“World-Honored One!
That Prince Reṇu had six other Kṣatriya youths as companions and friends with whom he constantly gathered and played, making mounds of sand.”

That minister, the Brahmin Sthira, also had a son named Vimalaprabha, whom he cherished deeply; he was of keen intellect and talent, such that there was nothing among the affairs he encountered that he did not penetrate and understand clearly.
“World-Honored One!
That prime minister participated in the governance of state affairs for many years. Later, at one time, he suddenly met his end.

When the king heard that the brahmin minister Sthira had already passed away, he was filled with grief, distress, and sorrow, his tears flowing freely. He beat his breast in alarm and agitation, falling into a stupor as if lifeless, and spoke these words:”

"This minister of mine possessed considerable talent and wisdom; he participated in the administration of state affairs as an excellent assistant and was constantly my companion in pleasure. Yet he has suddenly passed away, leaving me in deep anguish."

At that time, having heard that his father the King had already passed away because of the minister, the Brahmin Sthira, the prince was filled with grief and distress; overcome with sorrow, tears flowed from his eyes. The prince immediately went to where the King was, and upon arrival, he said:
"Father King, do not grieve, do not weep. Why do you harm yourself with such delirium and fainting as if you were dead?"
For what reason?

Your Majesty, the King, should know that the Brahmin Sthira has an eldest son named Vimalaprabha, who possesses both wisdom and talent and is moreover sharp and intelligent. If he succeeds to his father’s position, he will be able to manage state affairs; whatever his father understands, this son knows it all. Since such a person now exists, why does the King grieve?
"The King should summon him in secret and, according to the circumstances, instruct him to invite [the Bodhisattva], so that the office held by his father may be conferred upon his son.
When the King had heard this, he immediately commanded a messenger, saying to him:
"Go to the youth Gopāla and deliver these words:"
"The King now summons you; you should come here at once.
Having received these instructions, the messenger immediately went to the youth Prabhāpāla. Upon arriving there, he delivered the King's decree in its entirety:
"The King now summons you; you should proceed there at once."
At that time, having heard the words of the messenger, the youth Vimalaprabha immediately went to the king's presence.
Upon arrival, he extended his respects and was seated to one side.
Then the king, filled with joy, comforted and exhorted him again, speaking these words:
"I now instruct you according to reality: although you are grieving over the passing of your father, I shall now cause you to succeed him in his position as prime minister."
"You shall skillfully assist me in governing the affairs of state.

Having received the King's command, the youth Prabhāsa succeeded his father on the throne as a minister and governed the state affairs just as his father had done; all matters requiring attention were conducted exactly as by his father, without any deviation or error.
At that time, the brahmins, elders, officials, and common people of the kingdom, having learned of this matter, all spoke these words:
"How wonderful! O youth Prabhāsa!"
"In former times your father was named Sthira; now that you have succeeded him and are able to expand upon his previous deeds, we shall call you Mahāsusthira.
He whose original name was Rāhula was given this title because of the circumstances of his emergence from the fire; from this day forward, he shall be called Mahāsusthira.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the great minister, the brahmin Mahāsthāman, not long after becoming prime minister, immediately went to where the six kṣatriya youths were.
Having arrived, he said to them: ‘O youths!’”
"You should go to Prince Lainya and say to him:
'Prince! If there is any suffering or affliction, you and I shall share it together.'"
If there is joy, you and I shall rejoice together;
if you have a refuge, I too shall have a refuge.

Now your father, the King, has reached advanced age and his movements are frail and weak. Life, which is difficult for the world to know, may end at any moment; once he passes away, where shall we turn for refuge?

"You should know this now: there are certain ministers who, after deliberating together, have resolved that once the King has passed away, they will surely confer upon you the royal consecration. If you succeed to the throne, you must share the governance of the kingdom with me."

At that time, having heard these words from the great minister, the brahmin Mahāsthāmā, the six youths immediately went to the place where Prince Reṇu was. Upon arriving there, they related everything exactly as it had been told above.
Then the Prince said: "O youths!

On the day I am reborn, if there should be ministers who establish me as the successor and confer the consecration upon me, at that time I shall not forget you; I will share the governance of the entire kingdom with you, and whatever joys there may be, we shall enjoy them together."
"Later, after a long period had passed, the King, the Lord of the Realm, suddenly reached the end of his life.
At that time, the ministers and assistants went to the Prince's location; having arrived, they addressed him, saying: 'Prince!'"
"You should know that we, your ministers, have conferred the consecration upon you; the time has now come for you to succeed to the royal throne.
Then, Prince Reṇu said to his ministers and assistants:
"If you are able to establish me as the successor to the throne, and if I am indeed capable, now is precisely the right time."
At that time, the ministers and attendants immediately prepared an exquisite lion throne; the prince sat upon it, and they poured excellent fragrant water over his crown, saying these words:
"O Son of Heaven!..."
"The time has now come for you to succeed to the royal throne; we, your ministers, shall perform the consecration for you.
Once the King had been consecrated, he governed the affairs of state well.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
At that time, not long after King Līna had received his consecration, he enjoyed himself with the five sensual pleasures, sporting with complete mastery.
Thereupon, the chief minister, the brahmin Mahāsthāmā, went to where the six youths were and, having arrived, addressed them:

"You should know that Prince Līna has already received his consecration and occupies the royal throne; not long ago, he was enjoying himself with the five sensual pleasures, sporting with complete mastery."
"In the past, the King spoke thus: 'I shall divide the kingdom with you to rule.
You should now go to King Likhita and say these words:
'The King formerly promised us that we should divide the territory and rule it together.'"
"O King, can you now not forget?
At that time, having heard the words of the chief minister, the great and steadfast Brahmin, the six youths immediately went together to King Reṇu and related everything as previously described.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, King Līlāvaṇa said to the six youths:

‘In accordance with our previous agreement, I now record these words: I shall divide this kingdom and its territories into seven parts and give them to you six, so that each of you may rule over your own portion.’”
When he had spoken thus, the six youths together addressed the king, saying:

"If Your Majesty would confirm these words, it would be most excellent. We pray that Your Majesty will quickly summon the chief minister, the Brahmin Mahāsthira, and command him to delineate the boundaries according to Your Majesty’s instructions."
"That man is sharp-witted, possessed of clear wisdom, and fit to serve as a standard.
Then, King Reṇu commanded a messenger, saying to him:
"Go to the brahmin Mahāgovinda, the great minister, and speak these words:"
"The King summons you now; you should proceed at once to the King's presence.
Having received these instructions, the messenger went immediately to the residence of the chief minister, the brahmin Mahāsthāmika. Upon arrival, he delivered the King's message as instructed:
"You should proceed at once to the King's presence."
The Sūtra on the Discourse of the Great Firm Brahmin Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Upper.
The Sūtra on the Discourse of the Great Firm Brahmin Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Dharma Master Śīladharma, recipient of the purple robe and subject, and others, by imperial decree:
"At that time, the great minister and brahmin Mahāsthāman immediately went to King Reṇu; having arrived, he paid his respects and withdrew to sit to one side."
At that time, the king was filled with joy; he looked upon him, gave him instructions, and comforted him, while the minister likewise responded with solemn reverence.
The king said:
"O Great Firm One!"
"Now, for my sake, measure out this kingdom's borders and divide them into seven parts; I and six young princes shall each govern our respective portions.

At that time, having received the king’s command, the minister immediately measured and divided the boundaries of the land; in the far north, at the northern corner, the territory was vast and expansive.
In the southeastern corner, the boundary is narrow and irregular, shaped like a chariot.
In the central region, where many people gather, King Līnu resides.
In the kingdom of Kaliṅga, there is the city of Natabhūtra;
in the kingdom of Maśmaka, the city of Bhuvana;
and in the kingdom of Vandin, the city of Mahiṣmatī.
The country of Sauvīra, the city of Lāhūka;
the country of Mithilā,
the city of Vitihitā;
The great city of Campā in the kingdom of Magadha;
the great city of Kāśī in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Thus, these seven kingdoms were each divided into their respective boundaries.
At that time, the six young princes received royal consecration in their respective locations and each became a king, governing a separate territory.

From then on, there were seven kings, namely: King Līna, King Arindama, King Brahmadatta, King Vijitāvin, King Candraprabha, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and King Mahādhṛtarāṣṭra. Thus, these seven kings each ruled over their own domains.
Later, the six kings gathered once more and went together to the residence of the minister, the Brahmin. Having arrived, they said to him:
"O Great Firm One!
With the wisdom, counsel, and strategic skill you possess, you have assisted the great King Līlu; we six kings wish for you to assist us in the same manner as you do him."
Having heard these words, the Brahmin minister joined the seven kings in deliberating upon all matters.
At that time, the Brahmin minister subsequently instructed seven thousand Brahmins to recite those scriptures, and taught seven thousand Brahmins to read those scriptures.
At that time, all the elders, brahmins, officials, and common people, fully knowing and seeing such wisdom and talent in the minister-brahmin, deliberated among themselves, saying:
"This Mahāsthāman is truly a great brahmin; he is further able to instruct and recite the Vedic scriptures for the assembly of brahmins."
At that time, having heard the deliberations of the assembly, the minister-brahmin thought to himself:

"These brahmins, elders, commoners, and citizens have gathered here and there to deliberate, praising me falsely and claiming that I possess wisdom and talent, and even designating me as a 'true great brahmin. This is not appropriate for me; let me examine myself, and I see that I am truly not a true great brahmin. I shall no longer instruct these brahmins in the recitation of the Vedic scriptures; even if I were to know them extensively, it would certainly not be for my own benefit, much less so when my physical form and appearance in this world will not endure for long."

I have heard in the past what was spoken by the virtuous elders, the great Brahmins and wise ones: according to the Brahminical law, one should dwell in seclusion for the four months of the summer retreat and practice the meditative contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā-bhāvanā*). If that contemplation is perfected, the Great Brahmā Deva King shall manifest his presence and grant whatever boon is sought. Such a matter is what I desire; I should therefore practice this meditative contemplation as prescribed.

Having thought and spoken thus, the minister-brahmin, wishing to dwell in seclusion for the four months of the summer retreat to practice the meditative contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā-bhāvanā*), went to King Reṇu. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"I now desire, during these four months of the summer retreat, to dwell in seclusion at one place and practice the meditative contemplation of compassion;
I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission. Then King Līlāvaṇa said, "O Mahāsthāman!..."
"Do as you wish; now is precisely the right time.

At that time, having received the king’s permission, the brahmin minister went to a secluded place and, with a mind focused in concentration, practiced the meditative contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā-bhāvanā*) for the four months of the summer retreat.

When the four months of the summer retreat had passed, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight during the bhikṣu poṣadha, he performed the rites according to the Brahminic tradition at that very spot: first, he smeared the ground with fresh cow dung, then constructed a square fire-altar, and in the center of that altar, he further fashioned a hearth.

At that time, the brahmin minister bathed his body, donned fresh and clean garments, and ascended from the north to the southern boundary of the altar. He scattered auspicious grass (kuśa) to completely cover the ground of the altar, sat facing north, took up the sacrificial ladle (sruk), performed the fire ritual, and offered it to Brahmā.
At that time, not long after the Brahmin minister had performed the ritual, a great radiance suddenly appeared in the north.
Upon seeing this light, the Brahmin minister was struck with wonder; his hair stood on end with joy, and he became even more solemn and reverent, dwelling in a state of concentrated mindfulness.
The radiance was so blazing and intense that it had never been seen before.
At that time, not long after the Great Brahmā King had manifested this light, he came from the north and stood in the midst of the sky.
The ministering brahmin, with a heart full of joy, looked up into the sky and beheld the Great Brahmā Deva dwelling therein. He immediately joined his palms in prostration and spoke this verse:
“Your majestic form and radiant countenance are endowed with light; Who is this noble being appearing in the sky?”
"Though I see it now, I cannot know it; I only pray that you will explain it to me as it truly is.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King spoke a verse in reply to the minister-brahmin:
"Those pure practitioners all know that I dwell eternally in the Brahma realm."
"Furthermore, the devas know my name; you, O brāhmaṇa, should examine this for yourself.
The minister-brāhmaṇa then spoke in verse:
"The pure water and the seat that are required, And the honeyed milk-gruel, supreme among flavors—"
"First, I offer my wholehearted devotion; I pray only that Brahmā, King of the Brahmās, will compassionately accept it.
The Great Brahmā King spoke again in verse:
"The pure water and the seat you require, And the honey-milk porridge, supreme in flavor—"
“O Brahmin, you offer this first; I shall now accept it from you as is appropriate.
The Brahmin Minister spoke in verse:
“The realm of the five objects of desire is called ‘this world’; to be born in the Brahma-world is called ‘the other world.’”
"I rejoice in this meaning and have initiated this inquiry; I only pray that the Brahmā King will grant me his permission.
Thus the Great Brahmā King spoke in verse:
"Regarding these two meanings—this world and other worlds—ask whatever you desire and as you please."
"I now grant you leave; have no doubt at all. What you ask, I shall explain quickly.
At that time, the brahmin minister thought to himself:
"Now that I wish to resolve my doubts, with what subject shall I first question this Brahmā King?"
"Is this inquiry concerning the nature of this world prompted by something?
Or is this inquiry concerning the nature of other worlds prompted by something?
The Brahmin minister then reflected once more:
"As for the meaning of 'this realm,' it refers to that which is initiated by the five desires; this should not be asked.
I shall now question that Brahmā King regarding the meaning of being born into another realm."
Having formed this thought, he immediately asked Mahābrahmā:
"O courageous and pure one, Mahābrahmā!
I now question you; I pray that you will resolve my doubts."
"Among the Great Brahmās, if one wishes to seek birth in the tranquil realm of the Brahma-heaven, what practice should one cultivate to be able to attain such birth?
At that time, the Great Brahmā King spoke a verse in response to the counselor Brahmin, saying:
"To cultivate non-self is pure conduct; With the mind abiding in a single object, through compassion one attains liberation."
"Free from all defilements of desire and with afflictions removed, these beings attain birth in the Brahma realm.
At that time, the Brahmin minister addressed the Great Brahmā World-Ruler, saying:

"As stated in the verse spoken by the Great Brahmā, 'cultivating non-self is itself pure conduct,' I have already understood this meaning. That is to say, there are certain individuals who give rise to right faith, practice the dharma of renunciation, shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and abandon all wealth and pleasure."
Whether few or many, his wisdom functions accordingly.
Whether among high-born families or low-born families, his mind is equanimous and free from all attachment.
He possesses only the three robes and a single alms-bowl, having nothing else.
Among all the trainings, he teaches the methods of training; his actions of body, speech, and mind are fully pure; he sustains himself through a pure livelihood, free from all faults.
This is what is meant by one who cultivates non-self.
"Furthermore, as the Great Brahmā has said, 'the mind abides in a single object'; having heard these words, I also understand this meaning."

This refers to a certain class of practitioners of meditative concentration whose internal mind is pure, who abide in one-pointedness, and who—free from applied thought and sustained thought, and possessing the joy and happiness born of concentration—realize the second dhyāna and fulfill its practice; this is what is called the mind abiding in one-pointedness.
"Furthermore, regarding what the Great Brahmā has said concerning liberation through compassion (*karuṇā-vimokṣa*), I have heard his words and likewise understand their meaning.

That is to say, there is a certain class of practitioners who cultivate the practice of compassion; with a mind arisen simultaneously with compassion, they first direct this compassionate mind throughout the eastern direction—vast, perfected in its application, impartial and non-dual, immeasurable, and free from enmity or malice."

Having thus proceeded in the eastern direction, he likewise proceeds in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; throughout all worlds, he extensively exercises compassion and fulfills his practice in this same manner. This is what is called one who has attained liberation through compassion.
"Furthermore, as the Great Brahmā has said, 'One who is free from all defilements of desire and whose afflictions have been eliminated'—when I hear these words, I do not understand their meaning.
Great Brahmā, what are these afflictions?"
How can one cause the afflictions among human beings to become purified?
Within this ocean of afflictions that flows and surges everywhere, how can one enable practitioners to attain birth in that tranquil realm of the Brahma Heaven?
At that time, the Great Brahmā King spoke a verse in reply to the counselor Brahmin, saying:

“Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, anger, and concealment; Harassment, harm, deception, falsehood, as well as stinginess and envy— The arising of these defiled states and the slandering of others: These are called the various afflictions.”
By remaining far removed from such afflictions, one attains purity among human beings;
having blocked the source of the ocean of afflictions, one is born into the tranquil realm of the Brahmā heavens.
Then, the minister-brahmin addressed the Great Brahmā King, saying:
"Regarding the teachings on the various defiled phenomena as spoken by the Great Brahmā, I have heard their words and understood their meaning."
If I remain at home, I will be entirely bound by fetters.
If I go forth from the household life, I will be entirely free from faults; I shall cultivate the pure, bright, and holy life of brahmacarya. Why is this?
All that is born must perish; human life is brief. If one does not realize this, one will fall into the evil realms after death.

Therefore, I shall now know for myself and awaken within myself: I ought to practice diligently, cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) correctly, and no longer commit various evil deeds in this world.
"Great Brahmā!
I now renounce my home and seek to go forth into homelessness; I only pray that Great Brahmā will know my intention.
Thus spoke the Great Brahmā King.
"It is as you desire; now is precisely the right time.
Having spoken these words, the Great Brahmā King who had appeared in the air vanished and was no longer seen.
Furthermore, within the assembly, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Today, having heard this Brahmā King explain the matter of causes and conditions before the World-Honored One, I suddenly thought to myself: ‘Could that former minister, the brahmin Mahāsudṛḍha, not be none other than the Buddha, the World-Honored One?’”
The Buddha addressed the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, saying:
"It is so, it is so. That minister, the Brahmin Mahāsthāman, was none other than myself."
“I recall in the past the matters concerning the renunciation of that minister, the brahmin Mahāsthāman, and so forth;
have you ever heard of them? Pañcaśikha replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"I have never heard this before.
The Buddha said, "Pañcaśikha!"
I shall now explain this to you in due order.
O Pañcaśikha!
At that time, after the brahmin minister Mahāsthāmaka had performed the fire-ritual, he went to where King Reṇu was.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself and, with reverence before the King, spoke this verse:
"I have a wish that I now declare to you, O Great King Līnu, Lord of the Realm:
I renounce the position of minister to seek the homeless life; I pray that Your Majesty personally manage the affairs of state."
At that time, King Līna immediately spoke a verse in response to the minister, saying:
“If you lack anything you require, I shall provide all that you desire.
If anyone harasses you, speak at once; I shall punish them according to the royal law.”
You are like my father and I am like your son; as we assist one another, how could we ever part?
Though you serve as my minister, you are also my teacher; why then do you speak such words now?
The minister-brahmin spoke in verse:
"I have no lack of anything I require, nor am I troubled by others;
yet because I have heard these words of truth, my resolve for renunciation has arisen and shall not waver."
King Līnu spoke these verses:
"What truth is there in what is spoken by non-humans? For what reason should one believe and listen to such words?"
"Do not take these words as true—that you should abandon the position of a counselor and seek to leave the household life.
Then the counselor-brahmin spoke in verse:
"O Son of Heaven, I have first performed the fire-ritual, Bravely giving rise to a pure and focused mind."
According to the Dharma, he established the altar and performed fire offerings to the heavens, employing *śara* grass for the ritual.
The Great Brahmā, the King of Devas and Sage, manifested his form in response to my request.
Having heard his words of truth, I therefore firmly resolved to leave the household life.
King Reṇu spoke these verses: “As you, O minister, have so well spoken, I now am able to give rise to faith and understanding in all things.
Since you have heard the words of the former sages, How could this mind of renunciation ever be turned back?”
Your mind is as pure as space, And like a jewel of exquisite lapis lazuli;
Following your practice, I too shall follow, For it is because of you that I have attained awakening.
When King Līnu had finished speaking these verses, he further said: "O Mahāsthāman!
Your mind is pure and you delight in cultivating wholesome deeds; according to your wishes, you have a refuge, and I too have a refuge."
Then the minister-brahmin spoke again in verse, addressing the king:
"O King, you should renounce all sensory desires; he who clings to them is but a fool.
You should give rise to a firm mind free from attachment, endowed with the power of meditative absorption (*samāhita*) and patience."
This realization is the pure vehicle; this pure path is truly eternal.
This Dharma gate that has been proclaimed leads one to birth in the Brahma realm.
“Five-Tufted One!

When those six kings who ruled over the various kingdoms heard that the brahmin minister had abandoned his ministerial position and sought to leave the household life for renunciation, they immediately assembled the six kings together in one place.”
At that time, the brahmin minister went in person to where those six kings were; having arrived, he prostrated himself and addressed the kings, saying: "O Kings!..."

"You should know that I now wish to relinquish the position of minister; I pray only that each of you kings may separately seek those who can assist with state affairs, and that if there are those to be instructed, they shall rely on their own respective teachers."
I now desire to leave the household life to practice the Way.
Why is this? At the abode of the Great Brahma Heaven King, I heard these true words: that the phenomena of affliction should be abandoned and relinquished.
From this point forward, I take no pleasure in the household life with its constant entanglements.
If I were to leave the home life, being entirely free from faults, I shall cultivate the pure, bright, and holy life of brahmacarya.
Why is this? All that is born must perish; human life is brief. If one does not awaken to this, one will fall into the evil realms after death.
Therefore, I shall now know for myself and awaken for myself; I ought to practice well and cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) correctly, no longer committing various evil deeds within the world.
Then those six kings deliberated together, saying:
"For what reason has this counselor, the brahmin, abandoned wealth and honor to seek to leave the household life?
Among brahmins there are also those who delight in wealth and honor; we ought to exhort him with matters of wealth and honor so that he will not leave the household life."
At that time, after the six kings had deliberated together, they all said to the brahmin minister:
"We six kings have entreated you with all our wealth, honors, and every desire; yet, all the wealth and honors we now possess were obtained solely through adherence to the Dharma."
Having spoken thus, he immediately brought forth vast quantities of wealth, treasures, and all manner of articles of luxury and bestowed them upon the brahmin minister.
Then, the brahmin minister addressed the six kings, saying:
"Great Kings!..."
"Regarding these treasures and all such means of wealth and pleasure, I already possess them all in abundance; furthermore, whatever I do have was acquired in accordance with the Dharma.
Since I would renounce even what I myself possess, how much more so now that I am receiving these gifts from the kings?"
I am now resolutely determined to seek renunciation.

Why is this? Because in the presence of the Great Brahmā Deva-king, I heard these words of truth: that the phenomena of affliction (*kleśa*) should be abandoned and relinquished—and so on, as extensively explained previously.
"Pañcaśikha! At that time, those six kings deliberated among themselves again, saying:
'Among the brahmins there are also those who delight in beautiful and exquisite female musicians; we ought to give them to him so that he may accept them.'"
At that time, after the six kings had deliberated together, they presented a beautiful and exquisite courtesan to the minister, the Brahmin.
The king said:

"This courtesan of mine possesses exceptionally lovely features, a full and robust physique, and a graceful demeanor; moreover, she is highly skilled in the arts. You should accept her and not go forth from the household life again."
At that time, the Brahmin minister addressed the six kings, saying: "Great Kings!

My own household already possesses forty wives, whose physical features are exceptionally beautiful, whose bodies are full and robust, whose deportment is admirable, and who are all equally upright and graceful."
Even though he already possesses these things, he would still renounce them all entirely; how much more so now that he has received these royal gifts?
I am now resolutely determined to seek the going forth. Why is this?
I have heard these true words from the Great Brahmā Deva-king, namely: "The phenomena of affliction should be abandoned," and so forth, as extensively explained previously.
"Pañcaśikha! At that time, those six kings all said to the brahmin minister:

'If you now resolutely desire to seek renunciation, wait for another seven years; after that period has passed, once our sons, grandsons, and younger brothers have each reached maturity, we too shall follow you and renounce the world.'"
"You are most steadfast; if you have a refuge to which you turn, we kings likewise shall have a refuge.
Then the minister-brahmin said to the six kings:
"If one must wait for seven years, that is an exceedingly long time; I am now firm in my resolve and wish to go forth quickly."
Why is this? Because I heard these true words from the Great Brahmā Deva-king: "The dharmas of affliction should be abandoned," and so on, as extensively explained before.
The six kings spoke again:
"O Greatly Resolute One!
If it is not so, then wait for another six years, or perhaps five, or even down to one year."
The minister replied:
"If we wait for one year, it will be far too long; I am now firm in my resolve and wish to leave the home life immediately.
The six kings spoke again:
"If it be not so, wait another seven months.
The minister replied, "If one must wait seven months, that is an exceedingly long time; I am now firm in my resolve and wish to leave the household life with haste."
The six kings spoke again:
"If it is not so, then perhaps for six months, or even down to half a month.
The prime minister replied:
"If we must wait for half a month, it will be far too long; I now firmly resolve to leave the household life as soon as possible.
The six kings spoke again:
"If it is not so, wait for another seven days."
The minister replied: "Great King!
If you wait for seven days, that would be acceptable; as for my going forth into homelessness, abandoning suffering to pursue happiness, now is precisely the right time."

"Pañcaśikha! At that time, the brahmin minister went to the seven thousand brahmins who were teachers of the recitation of the scriptures and the seven thousand brahmins who were teachers of the reading of the scriptures; having arrived, he addressed all fourteen thousand brahmins, saying: 'Welcome!'"
Welcome, assembly of brahmins! As for all the Vedic scriptures you possess,
whether reading or reciting them, from this day forward, each of you shall seek out individual teachers to instruct and train one another.
"I have now gone forth from the household life; there is no one capable of instructing you. Why is this?

From the Great Brahmā Deva King, I heard these words of truth: 'The phenomena of affliction should be abandoned. Since that time, I have found no pleasure in the household life with its constant entanglements."
If I go forth from home, remaining consistently free from fault, I shall cultivate the pure, bright, and holy life (*brahmacarya*). Why is this?
All that is born must perish;
human life is short and fleeting; if one does not awaken to this, one will fall into the evil realms upon death.
"Therefore, I now know for myself and have realized for myself that I ought to practice well and cultivate the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*), no longer creating any evil karma within the world.
At that time, the assembly of fourteen thousand brahmins all said to the minister-brahmin:
"O wise teacher, you should not go forth into homelessness."

Why is this? For one who has left the household life possesses little meaningful benefit, little majestic virtue, and little renown; whereas those brahmins possess great meaningful benefit, great majestic virtue, and great renown.
Then the brahmin minister addressed those fourteen thousand brahmins, saying: "O brahmins!
Do not speak such words!"
Do not speak such words!
You should know that those who have gone forth possess great benefit, great majestic power, and great renown;
whereas the brahmins possess little benefit, little majestic power, and little renown.
Just as all that you Brahmins know and understand arises from the condition of being transmitted by a teacher, you should therefore not give rise to divergent views.
Then, those fourteen thousand brahmins all addressed the brahmin minister, saying:
"Just as our teacher has spoken, so it is; even so."

"Indeed, those who have left the household life possess great benefit, great majestic virtue, and great renown; even all that we know and understand has been derived from our teacher as its condition. If your teacher now has a place of refuge, we too shall have a place of refuge."
Then, the Brahmin Prime Minister again addressed the fourteen thousand Brahmins, saying:
"I have renounced the world to abandon suffering and follow after happiness; now is precisely the time."
Then the minister-brahmin returned to his own residence and went to his forty wives, saying to them: "Welcome, welcome!"
"Each of you should go back to your respective kinsmen, or else take pleasure in dwelling among other brahmin clans.
I shall now leave you, for my mind is set on seeking the life of a renunciant."
Why is this? From the Great Brahmā Deva-king, I heard these true words: "The dharmas of affliction should be abandoned.
From that time forth, I have no longer taken pleasure in the household life with its constant entanglements.
If I go forth from home, remaining consistently free from fault, I shall cultivate the pure, upright, and white holy life (*brahmacarya*). Why is this?
All that is born must perish;
human life is brief and fleeting; if one does not awaken to this truth, one will fall into the evil realms after death.
"Therefore, I now know for myself and have realized for myself that I ought to practice well and cultivate the true holy life (brahmacarya), no longer committing any evil deeds in this world.
Then the forty wives together said to the brahmin minister:
"You are most steadfast!"

When it was necessary for you to be a teacher, you were indeed a teacher; when it was necessary for you to be a husband, you were indeed a husband; when it was necessary for you to be a virtuous friend, you were indeed a virtuous friend.
"Now, according to your wishes, you have a refuge, and I too shall have a refuge.
Then, the brahmin minister spoke again to his forty wives:
"I am going forth from home to abandon suffering and follow after happiness; now is precisely the time."

"Pañcaśikha! At that time, after the brahmin minister had finished delivering his message in its entirety, for seven days he maintained firm and correct faith, went forth as a renunciant under the Buddha, and his hair and beard fell away naturally. The saffron robes were donned upon his body, and he became a bhikṣu, fully endowed with dignified deportment."
Once the counselor-brahmin had gone forth,
those seven kings all relinquished their kingdoms and likewise followed him into the homeless life;
all seven thousand brahmins who were his teachers and reciters also followed him into the homeless life.
Those forty wives also followed him into the homeless life.
At that time, there were again hundreds of thousands of myriads of people who, each rejoicing with sympathetic joy, all desired to leave the household life.
“Pañcaśikha! At that time, the great minister and brahmin Mahāsthāmā, having distanced himself from all desires, realized the fruit of arhatship.
Having realized the noble fruit, he further taught for his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life the various Dharma-gates pertaining to the categories of śrāvakas.”
Having heard the Dharma and understood its meaning, he shall be reborn in the Brahma realm.
At that time, the Great Firm Śrāvaka further expounded for his fellow practitioners of the holy life the Dharma-gate concerning the various types of Śrāvakas.
Having heard the Dharma, they understood its meaning and were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings within the desire realm.
Furthermore, there was another group of fellow practitioners of the holy life who, upon hearing the Dharma, attained awakening and were reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;

or another group of fellow practitioners were reborn in the Yāma Heaven; or another group were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; or another group were reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; or another group were reborn in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

“Pañcaśikha! At that time, if any man or woman in the assembly, or any fellow practitioner of the holy life, should conceive a mind of fault toward the Great Resolute Śrāvaka, upon the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into hell.”

At that time, among those in the assembly—whether men or women, as well as fellow practitioners of the holy life—who conceived pure faith in the Great Resolute Śrāvaka, upon the dissolution of the body after death, they attained rebirth in the heavenly realms.

“Pañcaśikha! At that time, the Great Firm Śrāvaka traveled throughout the realms of cities and villages, universally teaching and benefiting all—whether kings, ministers, elders, or brahmins, down to commoners and the general populace—causing them to abandon false paths.”
At that time, the kings, ministers, elders, brahmins, those practicing the holy life, as well as householders, and all the common people of the land, spoke thus:
"We take refuge in the Noble One Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the minister of the seven kings."
"How wonderful!
Today I have obtained a great and sublime benefit.

When the World-Honored One had thus related this account of past causes and conditions, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha felt joy in his heart; he distanced himself from worldly dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Origin Story of the Great Firm Brahmin Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Lower
